article.title: Polling is becoming more of an art than a science
article.subtitle: We asked pollsters what went wrong — and right — in 2024, and what’s in store for 2026.

extraction.summary: Eli McKown-Dawson interviews pollsters (Nate Cohn, Natalie Jackson, Patrick Ruffini, Andrei Roman, Mark Blumenthal) about 2024 polling performance and likely changes before 2026. Polls missed by about 2.5 points nationally and 2 points in the average swing state. That is slightly below average error, but it underestimated Trump for the third straight presidential cycle. The midterm polls of 2018 and 2022 showed little bias. Pollsters disagree on whether the Republican underestimation is specific to Trump or reflects broader partisan nonresponse. Big methodological changes are not expected, though more pollsters will likely control for partisanship through recalled-vote or party weighting. For forecasters, the article explains why heavy weighting reduces poll-to-poll variance, which makes herding harder to detect, and notes that Silver Bulletin pollster ratings will be updated.

findings.statement: In the 2024 presidential election, polls missed by about 2.5 points nationally and about 2 points in the average swing state. Silver Bulletin characterizes this as slightly below-average polling error.
findings.evidence_quote: the polls missed by about 2.5 points nationally and 2 points in the average swing state.

findings.statement: Polls underestimated Trump in three consecutive presidential cycles (2016, 2020, 2024), so systematic polling bias has run in the same direction repeatedly. The 2024 error was smaller than in 2016 and 2020.
findings.evidence_quote: They underestimated Trump for the third time in a row after pollsters spent the cycle trying to avoid that exact result.

findings.statement: Midterm polls in 2018 and 2022 showed little overall partisan bias. The Republican-underestimation pattern has appeared mainly in elections with Trump on the ballot, so it is unclear whether it will carry over to the 2026 midterms.
findings.rationale: Jackson's hypothesis is that Trump draws out low-propensity voters who don't vote in midterms.
findings.evidence_quote: The 2018 and 2022 polls performed well on this front, with little overall bias.

findings.statement: A 1-point lead in a poll should not be reported as a candidate 'leading', because that grossly overstates poll precision. Error much lower than 2024's level should not be expected. Blumenthal says being within about 1.5 points of the target is good performance given non-random samples.

quantities.name: error Blumenthal considers good
quantities.context: error relative to the true value, given non-random samples

findings.rationale: Polls no longer acquire effectively random samples.
findings.evidence_quote: Although headlines might tout a mere 1-point advantage in a poll as a candidate “leading,” that grossly overstates the precision of polls.

findings.statement: AtlasIntel's CEO argues the smaller pro-Democratic bias in 2024 may reflect luck from a tighter race rather than methodological improvement. A forecaster should therefore not assume the systematic bias has been fixed.
findings.evidence_quote: maybe that was actually more luck than a methodological improvement.

findings.statement: Silver Bulletin will give its official assessment of 2024 poll accuracy through an update of its pollster ratings.
findings.evidence_quote: For the Official Silver Bulletin Take, you’ll have to wait until we update our pollster ratings.

findings.statement: AtlasIntel is one of the highest-rated pollsters in the Silver Bulletin pollster ratings and pretty much nailed the 2024 results.
findings.evidence_quote: AtlasIntel — one of our highest-rated pollsters — pretty much nailed the results this year.

findings.statement: Judging polls by whether they 'call' the correct winner is misleading in close races. Polls should be judged by the size of their error.
findings.rationale: In close races, small errors flip the apparent winner.
findings.evidence_quote: often, polls are evaluated by whether they “call” the correct winner, and with such a close presidential race in many states

findings.statement: In 2016 most polls included too many college graduates, who respond to surveys more and lean Democratic. Afterward, the share of polls weighting by education rose sharply.
findings.evidence_quote: In 2016, most polls included too many college graduates, who are more likely to respond to surveys and also more likely to vote for Democrats.

findings.statement:
A Schaffner/Soler chart of national polls (July 24 to Sept 25, 2024) shows the share of polls weighting on each factor, 2016 vs 2024 (approximate):
- Age: ~87% to ~98%
- Race: ~94% to ~95%
- Gender: ~87% to ~95%
- Education: ~57% to ~83%
- Region: ~55% to ~68%
- Party: ~21% to ~43%
- Past vote: ~6% to ~33%
- Urban/suburban/rural: ~0% to ~18%
- Income: ~23% to ~18%
- Home ownership: ~6% to ~10%
- Marital status: ~11% to ~8%

A Pew chart shows national public pollsters rose from about 29 in 2000 (nearly all live phone) to more than double by 2022, with methods diversifying. The 2022 counts by method:
- Online opt-in only: 28
- ABS with multiple modes: 7
- Probability panel only: 7
- Other: 7
- Online opt-in plus live phone: 4
- IVR alone or with other methods: 4
- Live phone RDD only: 4
- Online opt-in, probability panel and live phone: 3
- Probability panel plus live phone: 3
- Live phone RBS only: 2

Pollsters use heterogeneous sampling frames:
- NYT/Siena samples from voter registration files.
- YouGov uses nonprobability sampling from an online panel.
- CNN uses a probability-recruited panel sampled nonprobabilistically for later surveys.
Because raw data are nonrepresentative, poll quality is now largely determined by the rigor of weighting.
findings.rationale: The RDD gold standard of high-response random samples no longer exists.
findings.evidence_quote: The distinction, in my mind, between high-quality and low-quality [polls] is the rigor of the weighting methods.

findings.statement: Cohn found that weighting to recalled vote would have made polls less accurate in every presidential election since 2004. In 2024 it appears to have helped in most states but struggled with changes in electorate composition, so toplines may have been better while crosstabs were worse. NYT/Siena does not weight on recalled vote.
findings.evidence_quote: weighting to recall would have made polls less accurate in every presidential election since 2004.

findings.statement: By Cohn's count, most pollsters were already weighting on recalled vote in 2024. That leaves limited room for further adoption, a ceiling on how much this technique can further improve polls.
findings.evidence_quote: most pollsters already were weighting on recalled vote by my count.

findings.statement: Silver Bulletin expects even fewer 2026 polls to lack a partisanship control (recalled vote, party registration, or similar). Ann Selzer's Iowa miss is cited as evidence that minimal-weighting approaches no longer work.
findings.evidence_quote: Ann Selzer’s miss in Iowa gave pollsters even more evidence that the old-school, minimal-weighting approach just doesn’t work anymore.

findings.statement:
Pollsters have proposed variant partisan controls:
- Cohn suggests weighting on past vote using a pollster's prior three polls rather than the last election's result.
- Jackson suggests weighting only the skewed subgroups (e.g., white voters) on recall, since subgroups are rarely equally off.

quantities.name: prior polls used for recall weighting

findings.rationale: These approaches avoid committing to the last election's outcome as the target and prevent extreme outliers.
findings.evidence_quote: pollsters might choose to weight on past vote across their prior three polls.

findings.statement: AtlasIntel attributes its 2024 accuracy partly to turnout modeling that anticipated a differential turnout advantage for Trump. Roman argues that recalled-vote weighting makes sense only if partisan turnout is expected to be similar, and helps less when one side is more engaged.
findings.evidence_quote: It makes sense to weight on vote recall if you think turnout will be more or less the same… between Democrats and Republicans.

findings.statement: Public media polls typically fix a weighting scheme in advance for transparency, while private pollsters adjust dynamically. AtlasIntel dynamically adjusts sampling and weights based on changing response rates late in the cycle, such as one side's supporters becoming more likely to answer polls.
findings.evidence_quote: So it’s quite important to understand response rates, and based on that analysis, incorporate changes in how you figure out your weights.

findings.statement: Herding means pollsters withholding results that differ from consensus, or tweaking likely-voter models until they match. Weighting on variables correlated with vote choice, such as past vote and party, reduces poll-to-poll variance by design. That makes low variance an unreliable signal of herding, and Blumenthal sees it as the main reason aggregates show less variation.
findings.evidence_quote: When pollsters weight on things that are correlated with future vote choice — like past vote choice — you’d expect less variance than you would with a truly random unweighted sample.

findings.statement:
Pollsters face competing incentives:
- Reputational risk encourages herding, especially in tight races, toward the average and toward 'no clear winner'.
- Trump's lawsuit against Selzer will likely make pollsters more nervous about releasing outliers.
- Some pollsters, e.g. those not weighting on education, may publish high-variance outliers because they attract headlines.
findings.evidence_quote: It’s easier to be wrong with everyone else and to say “let’s analyze what the industry did wrong” than to be wrong on your own

political_insights.insight: Pollsters disagree on whether Republican underestimation is Trump-specific or reflects broader partisan nonresponse among less-educated, low-propensity voters. Jackson leans Trump-specific, contingent on whether the 2028 nominee (e.g., Vance vs Haley) inherits his low-propensity coalition. Cohn and Ruffini see it as broader.
political_insights.evidence: Underestimation in 2016/2020/2024 but not in 2018/2022. Ruffini cites growing evidence of Senate polls underestimating Republicans. Cohn cites 2000s surveys with too many college grads in unweighted data.
political_insights.forecasting_implication: Uncertainty about the direction of systematic polling bias may need to differ when Trump is versus isn't on the ballot. 2026 Senate results will be a test.

political_insights.insight: Polls correctly detected movement toward the GOP among nonwhite and younger voters across recent cycles.
Questions on the economy, immigration, and Biden's approval, plus Harris's inability to separate from the administration, were leading indicators of Trump's 2024 win.
political_insights.forecasting_implication: Supports using incumbent approval and economic sentiment as fundamentals for the incumbent party's successor candidate.

political_insights.insight: 2026 is a midterm in which Democrats are expected to fare well.
political_insights.forecasting_implication: Consistent with a midterm penalty for the president's party.

references.description: Silver Bulletin pollster ratings (to be updated post-2024)
Pew Research Center, 'How Public Polling Has Changed in the 21st Century'
Brian Schaffner and Caroline Soler analysis of survey weights in 2024 national polls
Earlier Silver Bulletin article on herding before the 2024 election
Cohn analysis showing recalled-vote weighting would have reduced accuracy since 2004

open_questions: What the updated Silver Bulletin pollster ratings conclude about 2024 accuracy and bias.
Whether Silver Bulletin models treat systematic polling bias differently in midterms vs Trump-on-ballot elections.
How (or whether) Silver Bulletin detects herding given that partisan weighting legitimately reduces variance.
